title: Why hijab?
hook: women who tore their wraps to cover the same day; in the Qur'an hijab means a curtain, and modesty is asked of men first

segments.voice: Yesterday: shoes off, right foot in, and a few manners for a first visit. Your line was come in gently. Some mosques keep a basket of scarves by the door. Today, the scarf itself.

Medina. A verse has just come down, and the women who hear it don't wait for the market to open. Aisha remembered it years later, in a report in Bukhari: they took their outer wraps, tore them, and covered themselves with the cloth. Centuries on, the scarf is everywhere: on a goalkeeper, a judge, a girl in a school hallway. So is the question people ask about it, from outside and from inside: why? Today: hijab.
screen: `A VERSE COMES DOWN.` → `THEY TEAR THEIR WRAPS.` → `CENTURIES ON: WHY?`

segments.voice: The word itself surprises people. In the Qur'an, hijab doesn't mean a scarf. It means a screen or a curtain, something between two spaces. The verse about covering uses another word: khimar, a head covering. Surah an-Nur asks believing women, in Pickthall's words, “to draw their veils over their bosoms.” But read the verse just before it. Before the women are addressed, the men are: “Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and be modest.” In the Qur'an's order, modesty starts with men. Scholars set a minimum covering for men too, and a hadith calls haya', modesty of the whole self, a branch of faith. Then the ruling. Most scholars, past and present, Sunni and Shia, hold that adult women cover their hair in front of men outside close family. Some modern scholars read the verses differently. And within the majority view, the ways are many: a loose shayla, a pinned wrap, a turban style, a chador, and for some women a face veil, which scholars differ about. The journeys are many too. Some girls start young. Some women start at college, or after a hard year, or after Hajj. Some take it off and later put it back on. Many Muslim teachers say a scarf is not a scoreboard for anyone's whole faith. Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet ﷺ saying that Allah does not look at your forms or your wealth, but at your hearts and your deeds. So the lesson isn't about watching women. It's dignity: a modesty asked of both, and no one shamed for where they are on the way.
screen: `IN THE QUR'AN, HIJAB MEANS A CURTAIN.` · `LOWER THE GAZE: SAID TO MEN FIRST.` · `MOST SCHOLARS: COVER. MANY WAYS.` · `HEARTS AND DEEDS, NOT FORMS.`

segments.voice: Picture the faces you'll pass today, on a train, in a hallway, on a screen, and notice how fast the eyes judge: clothes, hair, a scarf or no scarf. On each breath out, let that judgment soften and let your eyes lower a little, the way the verse asks of everyone. Whatever you wear, picture meeting each face as a person, not a verdict.
Hijab. In the Qur'an, a screen or curtain; in everyday speech, the head covering many Muslim women wear; and a modesty asked of men and women both. Today's word.
Your line: dignity, not blame. Modesty is asked of both, and nobody is shamed on the way. Day one hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Many Muslim women cover their hair in front of men outside close family, in many styles and starting at different points in life; men are asked to lower the gaze and dress modestly too, and mosques often ask visitors to dress modestly.

original.note: Arabic: a screen, curtain or barrier; in the Qur'an a curtain, in everyday use the head covering.

trapdoor: what you thought: hijab is a rule about women's hair, full stop.
what it means: hijab — in everyday use the head covering; in the Qur'an a curtain; and a modesty asked of men first.
what a scholar hears: khimar in 24:31 and hijab as a screen in 33:53; 24:30 before 24:31; Bukhari 4758 on the emigrant women; the schools' debate over the face veil; Muslim 2564 on hearts and deeds.
